chapter_theme: At the Lord's assembly the king and the gods bow, a radiant god beside the Lord is named Civakan, and Sudharman tells how Civakan on the sandalwood hill cut the eight karmas and stood through summer heat, rain and cold to the end of his austerity.

cast.role: the king of the assembly who bows to the Lord, sees the god and asks Sudharman for the ascetic's story
the teacher, named in 3061, who answers the king and tells Civakan's story
the hero, now an ascetic on the hill
the radiant god seated beside the Lord, who 3058 names as Civakan
Civakan's wives, who come with the sons to see him
the kings who come to the assembly
the guards of the hill fields

3049.reading: The lord of the land, with women of lotus eyes, horses, chariots and elephants in his train, comes carrying fragrant offerings to the Lord's assembly.
3049.nuance: The Tamil never names the king; the next verses and the question in 3059 point to the king who hears Sudharman. Lines 2-3 compare the horses and chariots to something that gives out land, which is hard to parse.
3049.event: The king comes in state to the Lord's assembly carrying the fragrant offering (bali).

3050.reading: The king's host of banners, crests, garlands, crowns, umbrellas and troops fills the earth like a milk-sea poured out, outdoing the sea of milk itself.

3051.reading: Kings who gathered to hear the Lord of the pindi tree proclaim his good dharma freely left their retinues outside the golden rampart, out of longing for the flood of bliss.
3051.nuance: Line 4, வினையுடைத் தின்ப வெள்ளம், can be read as the bliss of those with karma or as bliss that belongs to the one without it; the sense is not fixed.
3051.event: Kings assemble to hear the Lord's dharma and leave their retinues outside the golden wall.

3052.reading: The king carries the bee-ringed flower offering, circles the Lord to the right, bows and praises the Lord's feet until the dwellers of the eight quarters marvel.
3052.event: The king circles the Lord, worships his feet and praises him before the whole assembly.

3053.reading: Like a coral-red fire in front of the sun, the lights of the sky-dwelling gods dim before the glow of the feet of the Lord who cut down his hostile karma, and the king looks on the crowd of sages.
3053.event: The king looks over the assembly of sages while the gods' lights fade beside the Lord's feet.

claims.claim: the Lord has cut away the karma that makes enmity, and his feet outshine the gods

3054.reading: Dazzled and taking a stern ascetic's shape for a god fallen from his path, the king speaks hastily without weighing what he sees.
3054.nuance: Who is the 'lord' of line 2 and who speaks the question is not settled by the Tamil; this reading takes the king as the one who 'says this' in line 4 and the 'unweighed' guess as his. The next verses answer it.
3054.event: The king, seeing a radiant ascetic, wonders aloud whether a god has fallen from the sky.

3055.reading: The speaker reports seeing a god descend in bright light and sit renouncing like a young sun, trembling at the word of the Lord of the three umbrellas, and bowing to him.
3055.nuance: The speaker is probably the king putting his question to Sudharman, but line 4 sounds like the narrator; the one who bows may be the god Civakan of 3057-3058, which the Tamil does not yet say.
3055.event: A god comes down from the sky, sits as an ascetic and bows to the Lord.

3056.reading: Sudharman tells the king that the dwellers of heaven, in the golden wishing-tree land of enjoyment, renounce nothing, and that nothing is seen except as the Lord's word has said.
3056.nuance: That Sudharman is the speaker comes from 3059-3061; in this verse only the address to the king shows a teacher is speaking.

claims.claim: those who live in the heavens of enjoyment cannot give anything up
nothing is seen that departs from what the Lord's word has said

3057.reading: Beside the Lord sits a lotus-eyed god whose very form seems to speak without his opening his mouth, and whose unfailing light is fearsome to look at.
3057.nuance: The verse does not name the god; 3058 does.

3058.reading: The speaker says of Civakan, whose chest is parted from Fortune, that his form and light have no equal on earth and that those who gaze on him with unblinking eyes find their minds changed.
3058.nuance: Naming the god Civakan Swami here answers the king's guess in 3054: the radiant figure is the hero, now seen as a god. Who says 'என்றான்' is read as Sudharman.

3059.reading: The king bows and asks Sudharman to tell, without fault, the history of the great ascetic and how he gave up his life.
3059.event: The king bows and asks Sudharman to tell the ascetic's story and his renunciation.

3060.reading: The great sage's words rain from the cloud over the ocean of unmatched complete knowledge, and the world drinks the nectar of the unfailing dharma.
3060.nuance: The rain-cloud picture is the narrator's praise of the sage; whether the 'great sage' here is Sudharman or the Lord is not fixed by the Tamil.
3060.event: Sudharman speaks and the world takes in his teaching.

claims.claim: the teaching comes from the boundless ocean of complete knowledge and nourishes the world like nectar

3061.reading: The gathered hosts, with the king first, praise Sudharman, the sinless teacher, saying that they would be of Civakan's company.
3061.event: The assembly praises Sudharman and wishes to share Civakan's fortune.

3062.reading: The poet announces that he will tell how Civakan suffered on the hill-top and how the young princes and the ascetic women went up to heaven.
3062.nuance: The 'I will tell' voice may be the narrator's or Sudharman's; verse 3063 onward is read as the telling.

3063.reading: Civakan goes to the sandalwood hills dripping with honey from the jack-fruit groves, so that the hill trembles with his coming.
3063.nuance: The speaker's closing 'என்பவே' (they say) marks this as reported story.

3064.reading: With a will that cuts the eight karmas into pieces, he becomes like gem set on gem and a sun that cannot be approached.
3064.nuance: Karma is destroyed here by the ascetic's own strength of mind, not by grace or by a god.
3064.event: Civakan cuts the eight karmas by the firmness of his mind.

claims.claim: the eight karmas can be cut away by an ascetic's firm will

3065.reading: The sound of waterfalls on the hill goes out in every direction and seems to call all to come, while on one side of the mountain he stands above.
3065.nuance: Lines 3-4 are hard to parse (a call 'come, fill up'); the waterfall as voice is my reading.

3066.reading: On one side of the hill, guards of the golden-bound millet fields drive back rutting elephants, and flung gems fly through the air like stars.
3066.nuance: The last half-line is cut off in the source, and the Tamil is hard to parse.

3067.reading: On another side elephants bathe in saffron, drink from honey-flowing springs, and dance with their mates and calves, without harm.

3068.reading: On another side striped tigers with their cubs sleep in gold caves lit by serpent-gems, while the kinnaras sing and show their forms.
3068.nuance: The peace between beasts is described, not explained; the verse does not say it comes from the ascetic.

3069.reading: On another side monkeys leave fallen jack, plantain and mango fruit, dance in the revel, and bathe in the honey-spoiled spring.
3069.nuance: The last half-line is cut off in the source.

3070.reading: In the four months of the sun's burning ring, as if it would scorch the sea, he stands on the elephant of knowledge beside a gold post, unmoved by the heat that spits fire.
3070.nuance: This is the first of three four-month seasons, summer (70), rains (71) and cold (72).
3070.event: Civakan endures the four hot months standing in tapas.

3071.reading: Like a sage-elephant, he overcomes the rains: clouds drink the sea, lightning frightens snakes, thunder breaks the ground, and sheets of water pour down while he stands.
3071.nuance: Line 3 ends with a full stop in the source and line 4 gives the subject: the subject carries over from 3070.
3071.event: Civakan stands through the four months of rain and storm.

3072.reading: When the four months of the cold north wind and mist have passed, he lived in the open field, and in these four months he guarded sweet life.
3072.nuance: 'இன்னுயிர் ஓம்பினான்' may mean he protected creatures' lives (ahimsa in the rains-retreat) or his own; the Tamil leaves both open. Line 1 and 2 are hard to parse.
3072.event: Civakan stays out in the open through the four cold months.

3073.reading: His wives and sons come to watch for him and worship his feet, and he, who would take the nectar-like food with difficulty, holds back the lotus hand and takes none; thus he crosses the sea of austerity and ends.
3073.nuance: The ending of the verse (அரிதிற் கொள்வான் ... கையினை மறித்துக் கொள்ளான்) can be read as a refusal of food that leads to his end, or as a gesture of withdrawal; the Tamil does not use the word for death by fasting, so I do not tag it.
3073.event: His family comes to him; he refuses food and completes his austerity.

links.note: 2846 names knowledge, faith and conduct together as the fire that burns the tree of deeds; 3064 has Civakan cut the eight karmas himself by the firmness of his mind.
links.teaches: The sermon gives the means of release as three jewels and a fire; the life shows the one quality of mind that does the cutting, so release is both taught and done.

links.note: 28 says only that Civakan goes to the ever-new state; 3073 gives the ending of the austerity by which he gets there, with his family waiting.
links.teaches: The opening summary states the destination in a half-line; the closing shows the cost, the family watching and the hand held back from food.

links.note: 2844 says release lies in the scripture of the Lord under the three umbrellas and the pindi tree; 3051 shows that same Lord preaching to kings who leave their retinues outside the golden wall.
links.teaches: The sermon only names the Lord as the source of the doctrine; the assembly shows what following him costs a king, who leaves his army at the gate.

links.note: 2843 promises that virtue makes gods in heaven; 3056 says the heaven-dwellers of the enjoyment lands renounce nothing and see nothing but what the Lord's word has said.
links.teaches: Heaven is the reward of virtue in one verse, and in the other it is a place where renunciation, and so release, is not done.

links.note: Kural 267 says austerity burns pain as fire burns gold so that it shines; 3070 has the sun's own fire ring burn on Civakan for four months while he stands on the elephant of knowledge.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the gold-and-fire image of austerity in general; the verse sets it in a particular season of heat and ties the shining to knowledge, not to appearance.

gains.a: the verse's four months of burning sun are given the principle that the heat is what makes the ascetic shine
gains.b: the Kural's gold in fire becomes a named ordeal, a season of heat with an ascetic standing in it

links.note: 3072 has Civakan spend four cold months in the open field, using the body up for release; Tirumanthiram 724 says if the body perishes the life perishes, so the body is nurtured to win knowledge.
links.teaches: One text treats the body as the means to be spent, the other as the means that must be kept alive, so they disagree on what a body is for.

gains.a: the verse's exposure of the body is set against a school that says release needs a body kept alive
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's nurturing of the body meets an ascetic who spends his on release

links.note: Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives sin out like a lamp but that sin returns when the oil of merit runs out; 3064 has the eight karmas cut to pieces by one firm mind.
links.teaches: The quatrain's lamp-and-oil picture makes the effect of austerity last as long as its merit; the epic claims a final cutting, so the two differ on whether it can return.

gains.a: the verse's total destruction of karma is tested by the rule that austerity only keeps sin away while the merit lasts
gains.b: the quatrain's returning darkness meets a claim that the cut is final

links.note: 3064 has Civakan cut the eight karmas by the strength of his own mind; Tirumanthiram 120 has deeds made into seeds that have touched fire and will not sprout, by the one who parts milk from water, the Lord or guru.
links.teaches: The seeds will not sprout in both, but one makes the ascetic himself the burner and the other leaves the burner a god or teacher.

gains.a: the verse's self-won end of karma is set against a Saiva reading in which the burning is done for the soul
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's burnt seeds meet a Jain account in which no one else burns them

links.note: Kural 261 defines austerity as bearing the pain that comes and causing none to living beings; 3072 has Civakan live four months in the cold open field and guard sweet life.
links.teaches: The couplet joins the endurance and the harmlessness in one definition, and the verse shows them in one season, if the 'guarded life' is the lives of creatures.

gains.a: the verse's four months in the open are measured against a rule that endured pain counts only with harmlessness
gains.b: the Kural's two-part definition is given an ascetic who lives it out in one cold season

source_issues: Verses 3049-3051, 3053-3054, 3058, 3062 and 3070-3073 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
3066 and 3069 are cut short at the end of line 4 in the source.
3065-3066 and 3072 are hard to parse; readings marked uncertain.
The ilampakam heading says 19/22, so the chapter ends mid-ilampakam; 3073 does not close the story.
